Living Well / Proposed experiment

Proposed experiment: simplify one part of your phone

Proposed experiment · 3 min read · Published October 8, 2026

On this page
  1. Choose one situation, not a total digital reset
  2. Protect the functions you need
  3. Record the change and ordinary context
  4. Look for costs as well as benefits
  5. Keep the conclusion proportional
  6. One question to take with you

By Nolan Kido · About this writing

A useful change is not necessarily the most restrictive one. Test whether one small adjustment helps in a real situation, and keep a straightforward way to reverse it.

Status: proposed experiment. This is a ready-to-try plan, not a completed trial, personal result, or claim of effectiveness. No findings are being reported.

Choose one situation, not a total digital reset

This is a proposed experiment with no reported results. Choose an ordinary situation in which an optional interruption seems to get in the way, such as reading or beginning a task. Describe what you intended to do and what interrupted it.

Do not start by declaring a target for total screen time. Time spent on a device can serve very different purposes. The question is whether a particular arrangement supports the activity and responsibilities you actually have.

Protect the functions you need

List care, work, accessibility, navigation, and safety needs before changing anything. Keep essential contacts and alerts available. Do not test a change that could make you unreachable to someone who depends on you or remove a tool you need to participate.

Choose a narrow adjustment you understand and can reverse. Device controls vary, so consult the current official instructions rather than assuming a setting name or behavior. This plan is not a device-specific setup guide.

Record the change and ordinary context

Write down exactly what you changed and when you will review it. During a few ordinary uses, note whether the original interruption occurred, whether you completed the intended activity, and whether the adjustment created new friction.

Record exceptions and reversals honestly. A day that required more device use is not a failure. Changing several things at once will make it harder to know which change mattered, so keep the first attempt small.

Look for costs as well as benefits

Ask whether you missed something important, spent more effort checking manually, or simply moved the interruption to another device. Ask affected people about any communication problem rather than assuming the change was invisible to them.

Stop or reverse the experiment when it conflicts with essential access, adds distress, or makes responsibilities harder to meet. You do not need to wait for a planned review date to correct an unhelpful change.

Keep the conclusion proportional

A personal observation can justify keeping a useful setting. It does not prove a general claim about phones, attention, or wellbeing. Note alternative explanations such as a different workload or an unusually quiet day.

Use the attention-check worksheet only if it helps you remember the comparison. The purpose is participation in life, not collecting a more flattering set of statistics.

One optional practice

Choose one optional interruption and one reversible change. Name what must remain available. Review the actual effect and restore the old setting immediately if important needs are not being met.

Keep any notes privately. Skip or adapt this exercise if it does not fit your circumstances.

One question to take with you

Did you become more available to the activity and people you care about, or mainly more occupied with controlling the device?
